Deaf
dĕf
adj. (unable or unwilling to hear; rendering Hebrew cheresh, Greek kophos)
From Anglo-Saxon deaf. Because in Hebrew hearing and obeying are one word, deafness becomes Scripture's natural figure for a will that will not submit.

Biblical Definition

Deaf in Scripture is both a bodily affliction and a spiritual condition, and the two are held together deliberately. The law protects the deaf man with a striking motive: “Thou shalt not curse the deaf, nor put a stumblingblock before the blind, but shalt fear thy God” (Lev 19:14) — the offence is possible precisely because the victim cannot detect it, so the restraint must come from the fear of God alone. That verse governs every cruelty done behind a back. God claims the making of the deaf as His own work (Exo 4:11). Isaiah then turns the word on the covenant people: “Who is blind, but my servant? or deaf, as my messenger that I sent?” (Isa 42:19) — the worst deafness belongs to those charged with hearing. And the messianic promise is stated in the same terms: “the ears of the deaf shall be unstopped” (Isa 35:5), fulfilled in the ministry the crowds summarized so well — “he maketh both the deaf to hear, and the dumb to speak” (Mar 7:37).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines deaf as not perceiving sounds, wanting the sense of hearing, and figuratively as inattentive, not listening, refusing to hear or to regard.

expand to see more

DEAF, a. Not perceiving sounds; not receiving impressions from sonorous bodies through the air; as a deaf ear.

2. Wanting the sense of hearing; having organs which do not perceive sounds; as a deaf man.

3. Not listening or regarding; not moved, persuaded or convinced; rejecting; as, deaf to reason or arguments.

4. Deprived of the power of hearing; deafened; as deaf with clamor.

Key Scripture

Lev 19:14 — "Thou shalt not curse the deaf, nor put a stumblingblock before the blind, but shalt fear thy God: I am the LORD."

Isa 35:5 — "Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf shall be unstopped."

Isa 42:19 — "Who is blind, but my servant? or deaf, as my messenger that I sent? who is blind as he that is perfect, and blind as the LORD'S servant?"

Mar 7:37 — "And were beyond measure astonished, saying, He hath done all things well: he maketh both the deaf to hear, and the dumb to speak."

Modern Corruption

Deafness of the will excused as honest doubt — and, in practice, the church's failure to keep Leviticus 19:14, where cruelty is restrained only by the fear of God.

expand to see more

Leviticus 19:14 anticipates the exact form most cruelty takes: harm done where the victim cannot perceive it. Cursing a deaf man costs nothing socially, since he will never know; tripping a blind man can always be denied. The law offers no external enforcement and appeals instead to a single restraint — but shalt fear thy God. That is the standing answer to gossip, to the anonymous word, and to every unkindness performed at a safe distance.

The spiritual sense is where the age evades. Refusal to hear is now regularly presented as intellectual honesty, and Isaiah 42:19 aims the charge at exactly the people most confident of hearing: Who is deaf, as my messenger that I sent? Yet the entry cannot end there, because the promise outruns the diagnosis. The ears of the deaf shall be unstopped, and Mark 7:37 records it done. The One who claims in Exodus 4:11 to make the deaf is the One who opens them.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew cheresh (H2795), deaf, from a root meaning to be silent or dull; Greek kophos (G2974), blunted — used of ears and tongue alike; the opposite of shama, to hear and obey.

expand to see more

Hebrew cheresh (H2795) — deaf; protected by law (Lev 19:14) and healed by promise (Isa 35:5).

Hebrew shama (H8085) — to hear, and thereby obey; deafness is its exact negation, which is why the figure carries moral weight.

Greek kophos (G2974) — blunt, dull of hearing or speech; the crowd's verdict on Christ's ministry in Mar 7:37.

Usage

"“Thou shalt not curse the deaf… but shalt fear thy God” — cruelty restrained by God alone."

"“Who is blind, but my servant? or deaf, as my messenger?” — the charge aimed at the confident."

"“He maketh both the deaf to hear, and the dumb to speak” — the promise recorded as done."
